ops.new_text: The representation fed to a clustering algorithm may matter more than the algorithm itself in unsupervised analysis of the electrocardiogram (ECG), and this study measures how much it matters. Several clinically interesting questions are unsupervised: which patients group together, what subtypes exist, and whether structure can be found without labels that are expensive or unavailable. A natural first attempt is to cluster ECG records directly. This study began as a re-examination of a master's project that clustered whole 12-lead records in this way. The project flattened each strip into a long vector, compressed it with a dense autoencoder, and clustered the code. It reported high cluster purity and a silhouette score of 0.89 [GAP: source of the master's project results]. The purity equalled the majority-class proportion in every setting. The silhouette was measured on a degenerate solution in which almost all points fell into a single cluster. The conclusion of that work, that the difficulty lies in processing the raw signal rather than in the clustering step, is the starting point that this study tests.

ops.new_text:
We chose the two foundation models by three criteria:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Both have public weights and take 12-lead input.
\item They differ in pretraining and architecture: HuBERT-ECG is a self-supervised transformer and ECGFounder a supervised convolutional network.
\item Both are evaluated in the closest benchmark \cite{lookingbeyond2026}, which reports ECGFounder's embedding as organised by clinical label and the embedding of HuBERT-ECG as organised by dataset.
\end{enumerate}
We included ECGFounder because of that report, so that the hand-crafted features are compared with a foundation model whose embedding follows the clinical label.
